question: Under the Firearms Act 2024, an Individual Licence can be granted for which purposes?
explanation: Section 28 lists three licence purposes for an Individual Licence: competition shooting, hunting and paintball. Collecting, dealing and primary production each have their own kind of licence.

question: For which purpose can a WA firearm licence never be granted?
explanation: Section 25 says a licence must not be granted to authorise possessing or using a firearm for personal protection, even as one purpose among several. The other three are covered by Individual, Primary Producer or Collector Licences.

question: A rifle on your multi-purpose Individual Licence is authorised for hunting only. May you use it in a club shooting competition?
optionA: Yes, any purpose on the licence counts
optionB: Yes, if the club agrees to it
optionC: Not until it is licensed for that
explanation: Each firearm on an Individual Licence is authorised for stated purposes (s 29), and WA Police says a hunting firearm cannot be used in competition unless it is also licensed for competition. Using a firearm outside its authorised purpose is unlawful use under s 219.

question: What is the most firearms a Competition Licence can apply to, before any extra allowance in the regulations?
explanation: Section 30 sets 10 for a Competition Licence and 10 overall for an Individual Licence; 5 is the separate cap for a Hunting Licence. The regulations can raise the competition limit in some cases.

question: What is the most firearms an Individual Hunting Licence can apply to?
explanation: Section 30(2)(b) caps a Hunting Licence at 5 firearms. The overall limit across an Individual Licence's purposes is 10.

question: Your Competition Licence already has 7 firearms on it. How many can your Hunting Licence apply to?
explanation: The overall limit for an Individual Licence is 10 (s 30), so 7 for competition leaves room for 3. The hunting cap of 5 does not help once the overall limit is reached.

question: A Competition Licence can only apply to firearms of which categories?
explanation: Section 35 limits a Competition Licence to categories A, B, C and H. Category D firearms are not available under it.

question: A Hunting Licence can only apply to firearms of which categories?
explanation: Section 41 limits a Hunting Licence to category A or B firearms, such as non-self-loading rimfire and centrefire rifles and break action shotguns.

question: Before a Competition Licence can be granted, the Commissioner must be satisfied that you:
optionA: Belong to a licensed firearm club
optionC: Have shot in an interstate match
explanation: Section 34 requires membership of a licensed firearm club, and WA Police asks for a club letter confirming membership with each application and renewal.

question: You have four firearms on your Competition Licence. To keep the licence, how many shooting competitions must you enter each 12 months?
explanation: WA Police's competition licence sheet sets at least six competitions every 12 months, six in total regardless of how many firearms are on the licence.

question: For what term can a WA firearm licence be granted or renewed?
explanation: Section 179 allows a term of 1, 3 or 5 years, chosen by the applicant subject to the regulations. The Commissioner can also set a term that lines up two or more licences held by the same person.

question: What does a Collector Licence for firearms authorise?
explanation: Section 66(5) says a Collector Licence for firearms does not authorise the licensee to use a firearm to which it applies. It authorises possession as part of a collection.

question: Under a Collector Licence, how many firearms can make up a firearm collection?
explanation: Section 66(2) says a firearm collection can comprise a single firearm.

question: What is the most firearms a Primary Producer Licence can apply to?
explanation: WA Police's Primary Producer Licence sheet sets a maximum of 10 firearms. Other licences the person holds have their own separate limits.

question: A category H handgun on a Primary Producer Licence may only be used for:
optionA: Shooting foxes around the lambing paddock
optionB: Guarding sheep from wild dogs at night
optionD: Target shooting on the home paddock
explanation: WA Police says the one handgun allowed on a Primary Producer Licence may only be used for the humane destruction of cattle, and only when incidental to mustering or yarding them.

question: Which handgun can a Primary Producer Licence apply to?
explanation: It must be a revolver of at least .38 and not more than .45 inches calibre, with a barrel of 100 mm or more. Only one category H handgun is allowed on the licence.

question: A category E firearm on a Primary Producer Licence may only be:
optionB: A cannon or a kiln gun
optionC: A flare gun or a line thrower
optionD: Any category E firearm at all
explanation: WA Police says category E on a Primary Producer Licence is limited to a paintball gun or a tranquilliser gun. A tranquilliser gun also needs an authorised person legally able to give tranquilising injections to animals.

question: A paintball gun on a Primary Producer Licence may be used to:
explanation: WA Police allows a paintball gun under a Primary Producer Licence only for marking animals or trees as part of primary production.

question: Can two different licences apply to the same firearm?
optionB: Only for spouses who share a safe
optionC: Yes, each for its own purpose
optionD: Only on a licensed dealer's stock
explanation: Section 172 allows two or more firearm authorities, held by the same or different people, to apply to the same firearm. WA Police calls this co-licensing; each holder must meet the requirements for their own purpose.

question: You are giving up shooting and want to pass your licence to your nephew. Under the Act:
optionA: It can pass to a family member
optionB: It passes along with the firearms
explanation: Section 177 says a firearm authority is not transferable. Your nephew would need his own licence before he could possess the firearms.

question: Your rifle is approved with an extra barrel in a second calibre. For the licence's number limit, it counts as:
explanation: Under s 107, approved configurations made by fitting an approved additional part are not counted as separate firearms when counting the firearms on a licence.

question: A Paintball Licence authorises its holder to use a prescribed paintball gun in:
optionB: Games run by a paintball business
optionC: Marking stock on a family farm
optionD: Games at a rifle club's range
explanation: Section 42 limits a Paintball Licence to games of paintball conducted under the authority of a Paintball Business Licence, using prescribed paintball pellets.

question: Who is eligible to be approved as an authorised person for a licence?
optionA: Any adult relative of the licensee
optionC: The licensee or a close associate
explanation: Under s 23 the licensee and close associates, such as employees, officers of a licensee company or members of a licensee club, are eligible. Nobody under 15 can be an authorised person.

question: Before a licence can authorise possession of a firearm, the Commissioner must be satisfied that you:
optionA: Have owned a firearm in the past
optionB: Live outside a town or city
explanation: Section 21 requires a genuine reason: the person genuinely intends that the firearm will be possessed for a purpose the licence authorises, such as competition or hunting.

question: Which kind of licence covers firearms used day to day in a farming business on land you occupy?
explanation: WA Police says the Primary Producer Licence is for people who use firearms in their primary production business, on land they occupy or control for that business.

question: A Hunting Licence for a firearm cannot be granted unless you have:
optionA: Land approved for hunting with it
optionC: A game licence for the season
optionD: A letter of support from a dealer
explanation: Section 37 requires land for which you hold the Commissioner's approval for hunting using that firearm. In practice that approval comes through a hunting permission on registered land.

question: How is a standard hunting permission issued in WA?
optionA: By a signed letter from the farmer
optionC: Over the counter by a licensed dealer
explanation: WA Police says standard hunting permissions are issued by a registered landowner or occupier through the WA Police Force Firearms Portal. They replaced the old property letter.

question: Who may give a hunting permission for a piece of land?
optionB: A ranger from the local shire
optionC: An authorised person for the land
explanation: Under s 39 an authorised person for land is the occupier, someone entitled to give permission on the occupier's behalf, or a person prescribed by the regulations.

question: Before anyone can hunt on private land, the land must be:
explanation: WA Police says all land to be used for hunting must be registered through the Firearms Portal by an authorised person, then assessed and approved; registration alone does not allow hunting.

question: A landholder plans to charge hunters a fee for each hunting permission. Under the Act this is:
optionB: Allowed if a receipt is given
optionC: Allowed up to a set amount
explanation: Section 39(6) says a person must not charge a fee for giving hunting permission for land.

question: Your only hunting permission is revoked. How long do you have to get a replacement?
explanation: WA Police says that if your only hunting permission expires or is revoked you have 28 days to obtain a new one.

question: You do not replace your only hunting permission in time. What may happen?
optionD: A move to a Collector Licence
explanation: WA Police warns that without a replacement permission your licence may be suspended and your firearms may be seized.

question: For how long can a temporary hunting permission be valid?
explanation: A temporary hunting permission is for short-term or occasional hunting, such as a visit or a trip, and is valid for up to 14 days.

question: A friend with no firearms licence wants a temporary hunting permission to join your trip. Can one be issued?
explanation: WA Police says a temporary hunting permission can only be issued to an existing Hunting Licence holder.

question: How must a temporary hunting permission be given?
optionA: In a phone call to the hunter
optionB: In writing, such as an SMS
optionC: Out loud in front of a witness
explanation: A temporary permission must be in writing, which can be an email or SMS, and kept as a record by the person who gives it. Standard permissions, not temporary ones, go through the Portal.

question: A landholder who gives temporary hunting permissions must keep copies for:
explanation: WA Police's property registration sheet says copies of temporary permissions must be kept for five years and given to police if requested.

question: You hold a standard hunting permission for a farm. Before each outing you must:
optionB: Plan to hunt in daylight only
explanation: A hunting permission is not a standing invitation. WA Police says express consent must be given each time hunting occurs.

question: Unless it is revoked earlier, a standard hunting permission stays in force until:
optionA: Your licence is due for renewal
optionB: The end of the hunting season
explanation: WA Police says standard permissions remain in force until the hunter's licence is due for renewal, and must be renewed along with the licence.

question: The farm you hunt on is sold. Standard hunting permissions issued for it:
explanation: When land ownership or authority changes, WA Police says any standard hunting permissions issued for that land automatically lapse.

question: In approving land for hunting, which location factor must the Commissioner consider?
explanation: Section 40 lists the size and location of the land, including how close hunting areas are to public roads and populated areas, along with the nature of the hunting and the firearm's capabilities.

question: Under the WA Police acreage guide, tier 1 centrefire rifles are generally linked to properties of at least:
explanation: The guide links 5 acres to tier 1 air rifles, shotguns and rimfires, 10 acres to tier 2 air rifles and rimfires, 50 acres to tier 1 centrefires, 100 acres to tier 2 and 300 acres to tier 3 centrefires.

question: A registered 5-acre property is generally considered suitable for which firearms?
explanation: In the acreage guide, 5 acres suits tier 1 air rifles, tier 1 shotguns and tier 1 rimfire rifles such as the .22 Long Rifle. Tier 2 rimfires need about 10 acres.

question: Under the acreage guide, a .308 Winchester is generally linked to properties of at least:
explanation: The .308 Winchester is a tier 2 centrefire chambering, and tier 2 centrefire rifles are linked to 100 acres. The guide says property size is only one factor.

question: Which chambering is a tier 3 centrefire in the WA Police acreage guide?
explanation: Tier 3 includes the .270 Winchester, .30-06 Springfield and the .300 and .338 Winchester Magnums. The .223 and .22 Hornet are tier 1 and the .243 is tier 2.

question: A landowner with a Hunting Licence wants to hunt their own registered land. Do the minimum acreage sizes apply automatically?
optionA: Yes, the same as for anyone
optionD: No, but each firearm is judged
explanation: WA Police says minimum land size thresholds do not automatically apply to a landowner who holds a Hunting Licence, but each firearm application is still assessed and the land must still be registered.

question: An occupier of registered land wants to hunt on it. Do they need a hunting permission?
optionA: They are taken to have one
optionB: They must issue one to themselves
optionC: They need a temporary one each time
optionD: They need a police permit first
explanation: Section 39(3) says an authorised person for land is taken to have hunting permission for it, and WA Police says this does not count towards the permissions they can issue.

question: An individual Primary Producer Licence holder wants to hunt pigs on the farm with a category C shotgun on that licence. Is it allowed?
optionB: No, hunting is A or B only
optionD: Yes, if it holds 5 rounds or fewer
explanation: An individual primary producer is taken to hold a Hunting Licence for the licence's firearms, but s 61(2) says it does not authorise hunting with a category C or H firearm.

question: A farm company holds a Business Primary Producer Licence. Can its firearms be used for hunting under that licence?
optionC: No, not for a company licence
explanation: Only an individual who holds a Primary Producer Licence is taken to hold a Hunting Licence (s 61). WA Police says a Business Primary Producer Licence does not carry that hunting authority.

question: You have three rifles on your Hunting Licence. What hunting permissions do you need?
optionB: One for each hunting trip only
explanation: WA Police says a Hunting Licence holder must have a valid hunting permission for each firearm on the licence, because the permission is the genuine reason for that firearm.

question: Which detail must a temporary hunting permission include?
explanation: WA Police lists the name of the person giving permission, the hunter's name and licence number, the dates, the location of the land and the purpose of the hunting.

question: What is the minimum age for a WA firearm licence?
explanation: Section 158 sets 18 as the minimum age for a licence or permit. Younger people can only use firearms under supervision in the situations the Act allows.

question: What is the minimum age to be approved as an authorised person for a licence?
explanation: Fifteen is the minimum age for any approval under s 158, and s 23(4) says nobody under 15 is eligible to be an authorised person. WA Police says this mainly allows an apprentice who needs a firearm for their work.

question: A 17-year-old wants to apply for a licence so it can be granted soon after their birthday. When may the Commissioner accept the application?
optionA: Only on or after the 18th birthday
explanation: Section 158(3) lets the Commissioner accept an application made no earlier than 3 months before the person reaches the minimum age.

question: Under the Firearms Act 2024, a young person is someone aged:
explanation: Section 5 defines a young person as under 18 but not under 12. No firearm authority allows a person under 12 to possess or use a firearm (s 158(4)).

question: To be granted a licence, an individual must live in WA and be:
optionC: Enrolled to vote in a WA seat
optionD: A WA resident for at least 5 years
explanation: Section 159 requires residence in the State and Australian citizenship, permanent residency or residence in circumstances the regulations prescribe.

question: If a licence will be your first under the Act, it cannot be granted until at least how long after you apply?
explanation: Section 170 sets a delay of at least 42 days for a first licence. Licences held under the old 1973 Act count when deciding whether a licence is a first one (s 433).

question: You last held a WA firearm licence four years ago. Will the first-licence waiting period apply to your new application?
optionA: No, you have held one before
optionB: Only if you are aged under 25
optionC: Yes, it is a first licence again
optionD: Only for a category H firearm
explanation: Under s 170(2) a licence is a first licence if you have held no licence in the 3 years before applying, so a gap of four years brings the 42-day wait back.

question: After your first Firearm Authority Health Examination, how often must you have another, until age 80?
explanation: WA Police's health examination sheet says one is needed every five years after the first, and every year from age 80. The regulator sets the timing through your portal account.

question: From what age must a firearm authority holder have a health examination every year?
explanation: WA Police says holders aged 80 or older must complete a Firearm Authority Health Examination every year.

question: The firearm authority health standards ask whether you are mentally and physically able to:
explanation: Regulation 221 says you must be able to continuously, safely and responsibly possess and use a firearm and keep complying with your authority's conditions, including storage and security rules.

question: You are charged with a disqualifying offence. While the charge is pending, your firearm authority is:
explanation: Being charged makes you an interim disqualified person (s 9). WA Police says the authority is then suspended and your firearms seized until the court process is finalised.

question: You are convicted of a disqualifying offence. What happens to your firearm authority?
optionB: It is kept but put on conditions
optionC: It lapses at the next renewal
explanation: A finding of guilt for a disqualifying offence makes you a disqualified person. WA Police says the authority is then cancelled and the firearms seized.

question: A violence restraining order against you lasts 2 years. How long are you disqualified in total?
explanation: WA Police says a disqualifying order disqualifies you for the full length of the order plus another 5 years, so a 2-year order means 7 years.

question: You leave an organisation that WA law lists as disqualifying. For how long after leaving are you still disqualified?
explanation: WA Police says members of a disqualifying organisation are disqualified while they remain members and for 5 years after they stop being members.

question: An old conviction for a disqualifying offence is now spent, so you need not usually disclose it. For firearm licensing it:
explanation: WA Police says a finding of guilt applies even when the law does not require it to be disclosed, such as a spent conviction. Only a finding that a court quashes or sets aside stops counting.

question: A court finds a person not guilty of a disqualifying offence because of unsoundness of mind. For licensing, that finding is treated as:
explanation: WA Police lists a finding of not guilty because of unsoundness of mind as a finding of guilt for firearms licensing purposes.

question: You hold a licence and are charged with a disqualifying offence. Within how long must you tell the Commissioner?
explanation: Section 197 requires written notice within 14 days of becoming aware of a disqualifying event, which includes being charged with a disqualifying offence.

question: You move your firearm safe to a different storage address. When must you notify the Commissioner?
optionA: Within six months of the move
optionD: Only if the police ask you
explanation: Regulation 240(4) requires a licence or permit holder to notify any change in the place where the firearm is stored as soon as practicable.

question: Your licence expired two months ago and you have not applied to renew it. What is the position?
explanation: Under s 179(3) the Commissioner may renew a licence on an application made within 3 months after the end of its term. The renewed term runs on from the old one.

question: Your licence expired five months ago. How do you get licensed again?
optionA: Renew it in the usual way
optionB: Ask your club to extend it
optionC: Pay a late fee to renew
explanation: Section 179(6) says a licence cannot be renewed on an application made more than 3 months after its term ends, but you may apply for a new licence.

question: You applied to renew before your licence expired, but no decision has been made by the expiry date. Your licence:
explanation: Section 180 keeps a licence in force until you are notified of the decision when the renewal was applied for before the term ended, unless it is cancelled or suspended.

question: While your firearm authority is suspended, it:
explanation: Section 204 says a firearm authority is of no effect while it is suspended, and it cannot be renewed during the suspension.

question: In deciding whether you are a fit and proper person, which matter does the Act list for the Commissioner?
explanation: Section 154 covers violent behaviour, family violence and intimidating behaviour. The Act also lists the risk of misuse and threats to public safety.

question: Under the Firearms Act 2024, a prohibited person is someone who:
optionB: Holds no firearm licence at all
optionC: Is on a good behaviour bond
explanation: A prohibited person is a person against whom a firearms prohibition order is in force (s 5). The Commissioner must not grant a firearm authority to a prohibited or disqualified person (s 140).

question: Besides a genuine reason, the Commissioner must be satisfied that the firearm itself is:
explanation: Section 22 requires the firearm to be suitable and appropriate for the use the licence will authorise, having regard to the purposes and circumstances of its use.

question: A rimfire rifle that is not self-loading is in which category?
explanation: Schedule 3 of the Firearms Regulations 2024 puts a rim-fire rifle that is not self-loading in category A. A self-loading rimfire is category C or D depending on its magazine.

question: A lever action shotgun with a magazine of 5 rounds or fewer is in which category?
explanation: Schedule 3 lists a lever action shotgun holding no more than 5 rounds in category B. With a bigger magazine it becomes category D.

question: A self-loading rimfire rifle with a 10-round magazine is in which category?
explanation: Schedule 3 puts a self-loading rim-fire rifle with a magazine of not more than 10 rounds in category C. Over 10 rounds it is category D.

question: A self-loading centrefire rifle is in which category?
explanation: Every self-loading centrefire rifle is listed in category D in Schedule 3. A centrefire rifle that is not self-loading is category B.

question: A tranquilliser gun is in which category?
explanation: Schedule 3 groups cannons, kiln guns, prescribed paintball guns, tranquilliser guns and underwater explosive devices in category E.

question: A handgun is in which category?
explanation: Schedule 3 puts every handgun in category H. The Act defines a handgun as a firearm reasonably capable of being concealed about the person that can be aimed and fired from one hand.

question: Which of these is a category B firearm?
explanation: A muzzle loading firearm other than a handgun is category B. A bolt action rimfire is A, a 10-shot self-loading rimfire is C and a pump shotgun over 5 rounds is D.

question: Which of these shotguns is in category C?
explanation: A pump action shotgun with a magazine of not more than 5 rounds is category C; more than 5 makes it D. A 5-round lever action is B and a break action is A.

question: Which air rifle is in category A?
explanation: An air rifle of not more than 0.25 inch calibre that is not self-loading is category A. Over 0.25 inch it is B, and self-loading air rifles are C or D depending on the magazine.

question: A combination firearm has a shotgun barrel and a rifle barrel. Its category is set by:
explanation: Schedule 3 places a combination firearm in A only if each part would be A, in B if at least one part is B, in C if it includes a C part and in D if it includes a D part.

question: A firearm that does not fit any category in the regulations is taken to be:
explanation: Section 8(4) says a firearm that is not in any category is taken to be prescribed as a prohibited firearm unless the regulations say otherwise.

question: A rifle is fitted with a device that lets its owner switch it to a mode that would make it category D. For licensing it is:
optionD: Treated by what it can become
explanation: Regulation 16 says a firearm with a function or device that changes how it loads or fires is categorised by what it can be changed into, so this rifle is treated as category D.

question: Which of these is a prohibited accessory under the Act?
explanation: Section 5 lists sound suppressors, bump stocks, folding stocks, detachable stocks and chassis carbine kits among prohibited accessories, and the regulations add more.

question: A bump stock is a prohibited accessory because it lets a self-loading firearm:
explanation: Section 5 describes a bump stock as a stock made or modified to let a self-loading firearm fire more rapidly than is possible with trigger-finger manipulation alone.

question: A sleeve fitted in the chamber so the firearm can fire a different cartridge is:
explanation: Regulation 10 lists a calibre conversion sleeve or adapter sleeve as a prohibited accessory.

question: A device fitted to the barrel to catch and dispose of cleaning solvent is:
optionC: Allowed if kept in the safe
explanation: Regulation 10 lists the solvent trap as a prohibited accessory. A licence covers a prohibited accessory only if the Commissioner approves it as a permitted accessory (s 121).

question: Which type of ammunition is prohibited in WA?
explanation: WA Police says prohibited ammunition includes tracer, incendiary and armour-piercing ammunition and a list of large calibre and magnum cartridges in Schedule 1 of the regulations.

question: Your Hunting Licence authorises the use of a .243 rifle. It also authorises you to possess and use:
explanation: Section 108 says a licence that authorises use of a firearm also authorises possession and use of ammunition for it and of a magazine that does not change its category.

question: You reload .308 ammunition for your own licensed .308 rifle, to shoot in it. Under the Act:
explanation: Section 117 says a licence that authorises use of a firearm also authorises the licensee to manufacture ammunition for that firearm for use in it.

question: You want to sell your hand-loaded ammunition to club mates. What do you need?
explanation: WA Police says reloading for your own firearm is generally covered by your licence, but a separate licence is generally needed to manufacture ammunition for any other purpose, such as sale.

question: You hold cases, primers, propellant and projectiles, enough to make a round. The Act calls this:
explanation: Unassembled components of ammunition means enough of the components to enable ammunition to be made. Holding them without the correct licence is an offence.

question: Which of these is not ammunition under the Firearms Act 2024?
explanation: Section 5 includes blank ammunition but excludes ammunition that cannot be fired, such as an inert cartridge, a dummy round or a drill round with no primer or propellant.

question: Which of these is a major firearm part under the Act?
explanation: Section 14 lists breech bolts, frames and stocks, barrels, trigger mechanisms, receivers and slides, and magazines. A revolving cylinder is added by the regulations.

question: You inherit a muzzle loading rifle made in 1860. You may possess it without a licence, but to fire it you need:
explanation: Under s 18 an antique firearm, such as a muzzle loader made before 1900, needs no licence to possess, acquire or supply, but its use is not authorised without a licence or permit.

question: Which device is not a firearm under the Firearms Act 2024?
optionC: A rifle that no longer works
explanation: Section 6 excludes industrial tools made to fix fasteners. A device can be a firearm whether or not it is operable or assembled, and air-powered guns are firearms.

question: At home, when may you have your rifle out of compliant storage?
optionC: When a visitor asks to see it
optionD: While it waits by the back door
explanation: Section 306 requires compliant storage at all times except when the firearm is in use, in transit, or in your immediate possession while undergoing maintenance, which includes cleaning and adjustment.

question: A level 1 storage cabinet must have at least:
optionA: A 2 mm body and 2 mm door
optionB: A 3 mm body and 6 mm door
optionC: A 6 mm body and 10 mm door
optionD: A 1.6 mm body and 3 mm door
explanation: Regulation 261 describes a level 1 container as a locked compliant container with a face at least 3 mm thick and a door at least 6 mm thick, or a locked Grade V safe.

question: A level 2 storage cabinet must have at least:
optionA: A 3 mm body and 6 mm door
optionB: A 4 mm body and 8 mm door
optionC: A 6 mm body and 10 mm door
optionD: A 10 mm body and 12 mm door
explanation: Regulation 262 requires a face at least 6 mm thick and a door at least 10 mm thick for a level 2 container. A Grade V safe also meets level 2.

question: Which of these meets level 3 storage?
explanation: Regulation 263 allows only a locked Grade V safe, a compliant secure room or a compliant strongroom for level 3. No steel cabinet meets it.

question: You store four category A and B rifles in the house you live in. What storage level applies?
explanation: Schedule 6 requires level 1 storage for 5 or fewer firearms of only category A, B or E, and WA Police's example of four A and B firearms at an occupied home needs no alarm.

question: You keep two rifles and one category H handgun at the home where you live. What storage level applies?
explanation: For 5 or fewer firearms including at least one category H firearm at an occupied storage place, Schedule 6 requires level 2 storage.

question: Two firearms, one of them a category C shotgun, are kept in a farm shed where nobody lives. What is needed?
explanation: Schedule 6 requires level 1 storage plus an operational level 1 or level 2 alarm system when 5 or fewer firearms including a category C are kept at an unoccupied place.

question: For storage rules, which of these is an unoccupied storage place?
optionC: A rented unit that you live in
explanation: WA Police says occupied means a home where someone normally lives; unoccupied includes a shed, outbuilding, business premises after hours or any place not continually lived in.

question: You hold category A, B and H firearms at one place. To work out your storage, use:
explanation: WA Police's storage sheet says that with more than one category you use the highest category when checking the storage matrix.

question: A compliant cabinet that weighs less than 500 kg must be:
optionB: Anchored to a wall or floor
explanation: Schedule 4 clause 4 requires a cabinet or container under 500 kg to be anchored to a permanent wall or floor, by bolts or coach screws or by chemical bonding.

question: Bolting a cabinet of under 500 kg, you must use at least:
explanation: Schedule 4 requires at least 4 anchor points, with at least 2 on one face and at least 2 on another face, each able to withstand 100 kN.

question: Under the storage regulations, a permanent wall or floor for anchoring a cabinet is one made of:
explanation: Schedule 4 defines permanent as a structural part of the place made of masonry, concrete, steel or similar material.

question: Which way of joining the faces of a compliant cabinet is not allowed?
explanation: Schedule 4 says spot welding must not be used on joints between faces. Butt welds must run the full length and folded joints must be stitch welded.

question: Can ammunition be kept in the same level 1 cabinet as your rifles?
optionA: Yes, loose on the top shelf
explanation: Regulation 261(2) allows ammunition in the level 1 container if it is in a locked compliant accessory compartment inside it, holding nothing else except permitted items.

question: Besides ammunition, what may also be kept in that locked compartment inside the cabinet?
explanation: The compartment may hold an unloaded external magazine, a major firearm part or another part whose removal makes a firearm inoperable, and a prohibited accessory (r 261).

question: A spare magazine kept in a firearm repository, out of the firearm, must be:
explanation: Regulation 280 says a magazine not within a firearm may only be stored in a firearm repository if it is unloaded.

question: Where must you keep the key to your firearm cabinet?
optionA: Locked away and out of sight
optionC: On a hook beside the cabinet
explanation: Regulation 281 requires the key or access card to be stored in a locked cabinet or container so it is not visible, and not in a place from which the firearm repository can be accessed.

question: A tradesperson must work inside your locked gun room. What must you do?
optionC: Lock up again once they leave
explanation: Regulation 282 bars visitors from access to stored firearms, but allows a service provider who needs access while immediately supervised by the storer or another authorised person.

question: Two licensed family members share one compliant cabinet. Each firearm in it must be:
explanation: Regulation 284 allows shared compliant storage only if each firearm is made temporarily inoperable, for example with a trigger or action lock or by removing the bolt or firing pin.

question: In shared storage, a bolt removed to make a firearm inoperable must be kept:
explanation: Regulation 284 says a removed bolt, pin or part stored with the firearm must be kept in a different firearm repository from the firearm. A lock's key or code is treated the same way.

question: Driving to a licensed range, your rifle must be:
optionD: In a case, loaded or not
explanation: Section 307 bans a loaded firearm in transit, and r 286 requires it to be secured against unauthorised use by making it temporarily inoperable, such as with a trigger lock or by removing the bolt.

question: You fit a trigger lock for the drive. Where does its key travel?
explanation: Regulation 286(1)(b) says a key or code for the lock, if in transit with the firearm, must be in a different package from the firearm.

question: Can ammunition travel in the same gun case as the rifle?
optionA: Yes, if it is in the magazine
optionB: Yes, loose in a side pocket
optionD: No, never in the same vehicle
explanation: Regulation 286(2) allows firearm and ammunition in one repository only if the ammunition is in a locked compartment securely fixed so it cannot easily be removed.

question: On a hunting trip you stop for lunch and leave the vehicle with firearms inside. What does the law require?
optionA: A window left down a little
optionB: A stranger asked to watch it
optionC: The case left on the seat
explanation: Section 308(1)(c) says a vehicle must not be left unattended unless it is securely locked and no firearm or related thing is visible from outside.

question: How must a firearm be carried on a motorcycle?
optionA: In a locked motorcycle hard case
optionB: In a soft slip on your back
optionD: In any bag with a padlock on it
explanation: Regulation 286(3) requires a firearm in transit on a motorcycle to be in a locked hard case designed for carrying firearms on motorcycles.

question: You are staying a night in a motel during a trip. Your firearm, when not in your immediate possession, must be kept:
optionA: Always in the locked car outside
optionD: With staff at the reception desk
explanation: Section 307(1)(c) requires the best location for safekeeping that is reasonably available to you. WA Police says that means the place that best limits the risk of theft, loss or misuse.

question: Under the Act, a firearm is in transit whenever it is:
explanation: Section 304 defines in transit as not being at an approved storage place for the firearm, so the transit rules apply on a hunt, at a motel or anywhere else away from home storage.

question: You keep your firearms in compliant storage. In law, this means you have:
optionB: Breached it if you leave home
explanation: Section 305(2) says storing a firearm in compliant storage is taken to meet the duty to take all reasonable precautions for its safekeeping.

question: You send a rifle by post for repair. It must be:
explanation: Section 392 requires a posted firearm or major firearm part to be addressed to premises where a firearms dealer lawfully carries on business, and bans ammunition in the same package.

question: Where CCTV is required at a storage place, how long must footage be kept?
explanation: Regulation 268 requires an operational video surveillance system to retain recorded video for at least 30 days from the day it is recorded.

question: As a joke, a friend points an unloaded rifle at you. Under the Firearms Act 2024 this is:
explanation: Section 295 makes it a crime to point any firearm at another person without lawful excuse. Being unloaded is not a lawful excuse.

question: When is pointing a firearm at another person not an offence under s 295?
optionD: When both people agree to it
explanation: Section 295(3) excludes pointing a prescribed paintball gun at another person in the course of a paintball game. No similar exception covers other firearms.

question: After a few drinks at camp, may you carry your unloaded rifle back to the car?
optionB: Yes, if you do not fire
explanation: Section 298(1) bars having a firearm in your immediate possession while affected by alcohol or drugs, loaded or not. Using it while affected is a more serious crime.

question: Under the Firearms Act 2024, you use a firearm when you fire it or when you:
optionC: Carry it unloaded in a case
optionD: Hold it while it is loaded
explanation: Section 7 says a person uses a firearm when they fire it or have it in their immediate possession while it is loaded.

question: Your rifle's chamber is empty but a magazine holding rounds is fitted. Under the Act the rifle is:
explanation: Section 7(2) says a firearm is considered loaded when any magazine that is part of or fitted to it contains ammunition.

question: A mate who has been drinking asks to hold your rifle. You should:
optionC: Hand it over without the bolt
explanation: Section 297 makes it a crime to give possession of a firearm to someone you know, or ought reasonably to know, is affected by alcohol or drugs, even unloaded.

question: When you have a firearm in your immediate possession, what must you do with your licence card?
optionA: Keep it at home in the safe
optionB: Show it within 7 days if asked
optionC: Carry it and show it to police
optionD: Carry it on public land only
explanation: Section 208 requires a licensed person with a firearm in their immediate possession to have their licence card with them and produce it immediately when a police officer asks.

question: Your licence is cancelled and you hold a physical licence card. What must you do with it?
optionA: Cut it up and bin it yourself
optionB: Keep it for your own records
optionC: Post it back to your club
optionD: Hand it to a police officer
explanation: Section 211 requires a person who stops being licensed through cancellation or expiry to surrender a physical licence card to a police officer as soon as practicable.

question: Your rifle is stolen from your locked car. When must you report it?
explanation: Section 393 requires a person who loses a firearm or related thing, including by theft, to report it to the Commissioner as soon as practicable.

question: You sell your rifle to another licensed person. What must you do?
explanation: Section 395 requires a supplier of a firearm or major firearm part held under a licence or permit to report the supply to the Commissioner as soon as practicable.

question: In a private sale, the buyer has applied for a licence for your rifle. Until the buyer is approved, you must:
explanation: WA Police says that in a private sale the buyer applies for a licence for the firearm and the seller keeps possession until the buyer is approved.

question: An online advertisement for your rifle must include its:
explanation: Section 389 says an advertisement for a firearm must include its type, make, serial number and calibre, unless the sale is under a Trade Licence.

question: While you hunt, a ricochet damages a farm shed. What must you do?
explanation: Regulation 238 requires a licence holder to report a safety incident within 14 days. It covers injury needing medical treatment and damage to things other than targets, gear or animals the licence lets you shoot.

question: You plan to take a licensed rifle to the Northern Territory for a hunt. When must you report this?
explanation: Regulation 239 requires the holder to report before the firearm is taken out of the State, giving the destination, the reason and roughly how long it will be away, and to report its return.

question: You change your email address and mobile number. When must you tell the Commissioner?
explanation: Regulation 240(2) requires a firearm authority holder to notify changes to name, residential or postal address, phone numbers and email within 14 days.

question: A Queensland hunter wants to bring his own licensed rifle to hunt in WA. What does he need?
explanation: WA Police says an equivalent authority permit lets a holder of an interstate or overseas firearm authority do in WA what that authority already allows them to do.

question: For how long can a WA firearm permit be issued at a time?
explanation: WA Police says a permit can only be issued for up to three months, and can be renewed for up to three more if applied for in time.

question: Across renewals, a permit cannot authorise possession or use of a particular firearm for more than:
explanation: WA Police's permit sheet says a permit cannot authorise a person to possess or use a particular firearm for more than six months in any 12-month period.

question: A visitor's home licence does not cover a firearm type they want to use in WA. Can an equivalent authority permit add it?
explanation: WA Police says an equivalent authority permit does not create additional authority. It only allows what the person's interstate or overseas authority already allows.

question: A miscellaneous possession permit lets an executor hold a deceased person's rifle. Does it also cover the ammunition?
optionB: Yes, up to 50 rounds of it
optionD: Only if the permit says so
explanation: WA Police says a miscellaneous possession permit for a firearm does not automatically authorise ammunition or magazines; they must be specifically authorised by the permit.

question: Your late father's will leaves you his rifles. Before you can possess them, you:
explanation: WA Police says a person may inherit ownership of a firearm, but inheritance does not authorise possession. The beneficiary must hold the appropriate firearm authority.

question: A licence holder in your family has died and their firearms are in a safe at home. What should you do first?
optionA: Move them to your own house
optionC: Sell them to a licensed friend
explanation: WA Police says Licensing Services must be contacted as soon as practicable, and firearms should not be handled, moved or stored without authority or advice. Call 000 if there is an immediate safety risk.

question: You want to close your firearm licence, which still has two rifles on it. What must happen first?
optionA: Hand in only the licence card
explanation: WA Police says a licence cannot be closed while firearms are listed on it. They must be transferred, sold or surrendered first, then a cancellation request is made.

question: A friend under a firearms prohibition order asks to shoot your rifle while you supervise. Is this allowed?
explanation: Regulation 247 says a supervised person is not authorised to possess or use a firearm if they are a disqualified or prohibited person.

question: Your farmhand wants to use the farm rifle under your Primary Producer Licence. What is needed first?
optionB: A quick lesson from you first
explanation: WA Police says family members and employees may possess and use firearms under the licence only if approved as authorised persons, which means meeting the same requirements as an applicant, including training and a health assessment.

question: You are taking a rifle out of the boot of your car. The National Firearms Safety Code says to remove it:
explanation: The Code says to remove a firearm from a boot or similar place butt first, never muzzle first, because people have shot themselves or companions by drawing a firearm out muzzle first.

question: Your shotgun is chambered for 70 mm (2 3/4 inch) cartridges. Which cartridges should you load?
explanation: The Code warns not to load 76 mm (3 inch) cartridges into a shotgun made for 70 mm and not to mix the two lengths.

question: Your box of cartridges got soaked in the rain. The National Firearms Safety Code says:
optionA: Dry them in a warm oven
explanation: The Code says never to dry wet or damp ammunition in an oven, a microwave or in front of a fire, because it may explode.

question: You want to check that a new rifle cycles live rounds properly. Where does the Code say to do this?
optionA: In the lounge room at home
optionD: At a range, not at home
explanation: The Code says never to check the action with ammunition at home, but in an area where it is safe to do so, keeping the muzzle in a safe direction.

question: Before loading a muzzle loading firearm, the Code says you must first make sure:
explanation: Before loading a muzzle loader, the Code says to ensure it is not already loaded, and never to double the powder charge or insert more than one projectile.

question: A muzzle loading firearm marked for black powder should be loaded with:
explanation: The Code warns that using modern double-base powders in firearms designed only for black powder may make the firearm explode.

question: You have loaded a muzzle loader but decide not to shoot. The Code says to:
optionA: Add a second projectile to it
optionC: Fire it or remove the charge
explanation: Once a muzzle loader is loaded, the Code says it should be fired or the charge and projectile removed, so it is never double loaded.

question: Among the seven basic functions of a firearm, to extract means to:
optionA: Throw the case clear of the gun
optionB: Push a new round into the chamber
optionD: Pull the case from the chamber
explanation: The Code lists feed, cock, lock, fire, unlock, extract and eject. Extracting removes the fired or unfired case from the chamber; ejecting throws it clear.

question: Among the seven basic functions of a firearm, to feed means to:
optionA: Put a round into the chamber
optionC: Hold the bolt to the breech
explanation: Feeding inserts a live round or cartridge into the chamber. Locking holds the bolt tight to the breech, and firing discharges one round.

question: On a closed-cocked self-loading firearm, after each shot the firearm is:
explanation: The Code explains that a closed-cocked self-loader moves its bolt forward to feed the next round after each shot, leaving the firearm loaded, cocked and ready to fire again.

question: On an open-cocked self-loading firearm, after a shot the bolt:
explanation: In the open-cocked type the bolt remains to the rear after firing; squeezing the trigger sends it forward to feed and fire the next round.

question: You load a break-open shotgun and close the barrels so the action locks. The Code says the shotgun is now:
explanation: The Code says that once the barrels are closed and the action locks, the shotgun is loaded and ready to fire, and extreme caution is needed at that point.

question: Before putting a firearm away, what does the Code say never to do to the barrel?
explanation: The Code says never to block the barrel when storing a firearm; make sure it is clean and coat the firearm lightly with oil.

question: Storing a lever action, pump action or self-loading firearm, the Code says you should:
explanation: The Code says to remove the bolt and magazine where possible, but not to try to remove the action from lever, pump or self-loading firearms.

question: In the National Firearms Safety Code's glossary, a hang-fire is:
optionD: A bullet left in the bore
explanation: A hang-fire is ignition that is delayed beyond the normal time after the firing pin strikes the primer, which is why a firearm that fails to fire must stay pointed safely.

question: In the Code's glossary, headspace is the space between:
explanation: Headspace is the distance between the base of the chambered cartridge and the face of the bolt or breech block with the action closed. A gunsmith checks it.

question: You no longer want one of your firearms. The Code says to dispose of it lawfully by:
explanation: Principle 16 says to surrender unwanted firearms to the police or sell them to or through a licensed dealer. Supplying to an unlicensed person is an offence.

question: How many basic functions does the National Firearms Safety Code say a firearm goes through each time it is loaded and fired?
explanation: The Code describes seven functions: feed, cock, lock, fire, unlock, extract and eject, though in some firearms not every step is obvious.

question: In a centrefire cartridge, the primer sits:
optionA: Around the rim of the case
optionC: In the middle of the base
explanation: A centrefire cartridge has a separate primer seated in a pocket in the centre of the base. A rimfire has its priming compound in the rim.

question: In the Code's glossary, a shotgun's gauge is worked out from:
explanation: Gauge is measured by the number of solid lead balls of the bore's diameter that can be made from one pound of lead, so a smaller number means a bigger bore.

question: In the Code's glossary, calibre means:
explanation: Calibre is the nominal diameter of the bore of a firearm, or of the bullet or projectile it fires.

question: In the Code's glossary, the lands of a rifle barrel are:
explanation: Lands are the raised portions of the bore between the rifling grooves. Together they spin the projectile.

question: In the phrase 'lock, stock and barrel', the lock is now more commonly called:
explanation: The Code explains that the lock is the mechanism that fires the cartridge, now more commonly called the action. The stock is the butt and fore-end.

question: On a bolt action firearm, lifting the bolt handle:
explanation: The Code's bolt action sequence locks the action when the bolt handle is lowered and unlocks it when the handle is lifted, before the bolt is pulled back to extract and eject.

question: In the Code's glossary, a clip is:
explanation: A clip is a device that holds a number of cartridges together for easy or quick loading, as opposed to a magazine, which holds cartridges in or on the firearm.

question: You hold a Hunting Licence and a hunting permission for a farm. Where may you sight in your rifle?
optionA: Where it may be used to hunt
optionB: Only at a licensed firearm range
optionC: Only with a police range permit
explanation: Section 111 lets a Hunting Licence holder target shoot to sight in a firearm at any location where the licence otherwise authorises its use. Section 110 also allows sighting in at a licensed range.

question: Your licence lets you target shoot at licensed firearm ranges, but not at which kind of range?
explanation: Regulation 248 says a licence or permit that authorises use at a licensed firearm range does not authorise use at a range that is a shooting gallery.

question: At a licensed firearm range, your Hunting Licence also lets you:
optionB: Hire your rifle out to others
explanation: Section 110 adds target shooting, including sighting in, and firearms training from an approved firearms trainer at a licensed range. Competitions need a Competition Licence.

question: Before using your firearm at a licensed range under your own licence, you need:
explanation: Section 81 says a licence other than a Range Licence authorises use at a licensed firearm range only with range permission from an authorised person for that Range Licence.

question: The regulations can set rules for target shooting under a licence. These can cover:
optionC: How many shots you may fire
optionD: The weather on the shooting day
explanation: Section 126 lets the regulations set target shooting requirements, including the size and material of targets, their position and nearness to roads, and target backstops.

question: A shooter fires near a neighbour's house to frighten them off a boundary. Under s 296 this is:
optionD: Legal if no one is hurt
explanation: Section 296 makes it a crime to fire a firearm to the danger of, or in a way likely to cause fear to, the public or any person.

question: A hunter says their Biodiversity Conservation Act authority lets them shoot on a farm without the occupier's consent. Under s 300:
optionC: It is not a lawful excuse
explanation: Section 300(3) says using or carrying a firearm for an activity authorised under the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016 is not a lawful excuse for the trespass offences.

question: A rabbit sits on the far side of a gravel road from you. Firing across the road is:
optionA: Fine if no traffic is coming
optionB: Fine on an unsealed back road
explanation: Section 299 makes it a crime to fire a firearm, or a projectile from one, onto, from or across any road or public place without lawful excuse.

question: You shoot a fox under your Hunting Licence. Must you report it to the Commissioner as a safety incident?
explanation: Regulation 238 excludes damage the licence authorises, and gives the death of an animal under a Hunting Licence as an example. Injuries needing medical treatment must be reported.

question: For a young person using a firearm, immediate supervision means the supervisor is:
optionB: Present and able to step in
explanation: WA Police defines immediate supervision as the supervisor being present, able to see and hear the activity, and able to intervene quickly if needed.

question: A 14-year-old will use your firearm under your Individual Licence. Who must supervise them?
explanation: Section 31 authorises the same use of the firearm by a young person under the immediate supervision of the licensee, so the licensee does the supervising.

question: To supervise a young person under your Individual Licence, you must have held that licence for at least:
explanation: Section 31 requires the licensee to have held an Individual Licence for a continuous period of not less than 5 years.

question: Your 15-year-old nephew wants to shoot rabbits with your rifle, which is licensed for competition only. Can he, under your supervision?
optionA: No, it is not licensed to hunt
optionD: Yes, if he fires only a few shots
explanation: A young person may only use the firearm for what the licence authorises for that firearm, under immediate supervision. A competition-only firearm cannot be used for hunting.

question: A 13-year-old wants to use a club firearm at a licensed range. Who must supervise?
optionA: Any club member who is there
explanation: WA Police says a young person may use a club or range firearm at a licensed range under the immediate supervision of an authorised person for the Club or Range Licence, with parental consent.

question: At a licensed club range, what is needed before a 13-year-old may shoot?
optionB: A phone call from a parent
explanation: For a young person aged 12 to under 16, WA Police says a parent must give written consent and stay at the licensed range while the young person uses the firearm.

question: A 16-year-old has written parental consent to shoot a club firearm. Must the parent stay at the range?
explanation: WA Police says a young person aged 16 to under 18 needs a parent's written consent, but the rule that the parent stays at the range applies only to those aged 12 to under 16.

question: A 14-year-old on the family farm uses firearms under the parent's Primary Producer Licence. Which categories may they use?
explanation: WA Police says this arrangement covers only category A, B and E firearms; s 62(3) says the licence does not authorise a young person to use a category C or H firearm.

question: For every young person playing at a licensed paintball business, a parent must also declare that the young person:
optionA: Has done a firearm safety course
explanation: WA Police says the parent must declare to the Paintball Business Licensee that the young person is not a disqualified person or prohibited person, as well as giving the consent required for their age.

question: To use a firearm on someone else's land, the Act requires:
explanation: Section 300(1) makes it an offence to use a firearm on land belonging to another person without the express consent of the occupier or someone apparently authorised to act for them.

question: You walk across a neighbour's paddock with a cased rifle to reach your permission land. Under the Act you need:
optionB: Nothing if it is in a case
explanation: Section 300(2) makes it an offence to carry a firearm onto or across land used for primary production, other than on a public road, without the occupier's express consent.
